name: The Great Yew of Ormiston

location.address: Ormiston Hall grounds, Ormiston, East Lothian EH35
location.neighbourhood: Ormiston, East Lothian (day-trip distance from Edinburgh, ~16.7km)

access: Free, no fees or set hours. Scotland's Yew Tree Heritage Initiative (SYTHI) records access as public. The yew stands on the former grounds of Ormiston Hall, now partly a housing development at Ormiston village; reached via a marked path off the Ormiston Hall driveway, past the hall ruins. Ancient Yew Group's 2001 site visit called it a private estate with unclear ownership and difficult to locate; SYTHI's page (which carries the precise coordinate and a current access line) supersedes that as the more recent, specific source, so this is delivered as a day-trip out of Edinburgh rather than an in-town tree.
transport: No direct rail link. By car via the A6093 (Ormiston village, ~16.7km / c.25 min drive from Edinburgh centre); day bus services run from Edinburgh/Tranent to Ormiston village, then roughly 15-20 minutes on foot to the site (no specific verified route number, N113 is a night-only service to Ormiston).
verify_notes: TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES for existence/species/rough age: Scotland's Yew Tree Heritage Initiative (SYTHI) and Ancient Yew Group (AYG), both dedicated yew-recording bodies; also documented on Wikipedia, Ancient Tree Forum and multiple press pieces. ALIVE NOW: East Lothian Courier reported vandalism (carved initials) on 'The Great Yew of Ormiston' in a recent, undated-but-current article, which is itself proof of a living standing tree being damaged, not a memorial. AGE: sources agree only on 'over 1,000 years' / 'Ancient Exceptional (more than 1000 yrs)' (SYTHI) and 'could well be around a thousand years old' (AYG); this is a vague age from real sources, repeated as vaguely as given, not sharpened to a number I cannot support. Recorded age_min/max as a broad band (500-1000) reflecting that even the sources hedge with 'could well be'; do not read either bound as precise. GIRTH: AYG's site database records the main 'Ancient' yew at 503cm girth at 30cm height (2013 survey); a separate quoted figure of 592cm at 100cm height appears in some secondary summaries, so there is a genuine unresolved DISAGREEMENT on the exact girth measurement height/value, likely because the tree has several major stems from layering (AYG also records two further stems on site at 356cm and 313cm). Do not treat 503cm as the only true figure; flag this. HISTORY: first mentioned in text in 1474 (a document reportedly signed beneath the largest yew that year); traditionally associated with reformer John Knox, who is said to have been present in 1545 when his companion George Wishart was captured near/under the tree during the Scottish Reformation (per Ancient Tree Forum, Knox's presence is oral tradition rather than a primary-sourced fact, flagged as such by commenters on that same page). Known locally as the 'Cathedral Yew' because its layering branches root and re-sprout around a hollow core, forming a ring like a natural cathedral: a genuinely rare growth form in Scotland (AYG calls layering yews 'few' nationally). LOCATION: SYTHI gives a specific coordinate (55.898018, -2.942109) for the tree itself, distinct from and more precise than the lead's original coordinate (55.89788, -2.9402), which sits about 130m away; used SYTHI's tree-level coordinate as CONFIRMED. ACCESS is the one real open question: AYG's field note (from a site visit on 27-Jul-2001) describes a private estate, unclear ownership, hard to find; SYTHI (a more recent, yew-specialist source with a photographed access route and precise coordinate) states plainly 'Access: Public - No fees nor times apply'. Treated SYTHI as controlling since it is more current and more specific, but flagged curation_status because the two sources disagree on the access question rather than just corroborating each other.

name: The Gilwell Oak

location.address: Gilwell Park, Bury Road, Chingford, London E4 7QW (near the Training Ground / Syd Kesseler Centre)
location.neighbourhood: Chingford, on the edge of Epping Forest (~18.2km from central London)

access: Free to explore for the day, no advance booking needed for a casual heritage visit: Scout Adventures' own current visiting page (archived 4 March 2026) says the grounds are open 7 days a week except a Christmas closure and days with large events, and asks day visitors only to check in at the Scout Adventures Reception in the Syd Kesseler Centre on arrival. FLAGGED CAVEAT: an Epping Forest District Council document (sourced to a 1998 guidebook, itself citing a 2008 survey) instead states 'access to the tree is by appointment only, as this site is a training complex for the Scouting Movement.' The two disagree; treated the operator's own current page as controlling since it is newer and site-specific, but note this before publishing in case the reception check-in is stricter than a drop-in visit in practice.
transport: Chingford railway station (London Overground, London Liverpool Street line), then about a 30 minute walk to Gilwell Park along a busy road with only a partial footpath, or a taxi from the station.
verify_notes: TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES for existence and species: Wikipedia's Gilwell Oak article and the Woodland Trust's Tree of the Year contest microsite (treeoftheyear.org), both describing the same Quercus robur at Gilwell Park; a third, the Epping Forest Guardian, corroborates via a 2018 news story about the tree winning free 'Tree Rescue' revitalisation treatment. ALIVE: the 2018 Tree Rescue story (biochar and soil de-compaction treatment after the head gardener nominated it as 'a bit worse for wear') is the most recent dated confirmation found; no later news found in this pass, so if a fresher sighting exists it was not seen here. AGE has a real disagreement: Epping Forest Guardian (2018) and treeoftheyear.org (2018) both independently give 450-500 / 450-550 years, quoting the site's own head gardener in the Guardian's case; Grokipedia's page (an AI-generated tertiary source, treated with caution) instead states 'approximately 350 years old based on a 2017 health survey' with no traceable citation for that figure, and separately claims 'the current tree is the second to bear this name, with the original located in a nearby field.' Neither of Grokipedia's two claims could be corroborated in this pass; used the two-newspaper/contest-site figure (450-550) as the delivered band and flagged the discrepancy rather than silently picking a winner, per the register-pitfalls rule on conflicting sources. GIRTH: 4.80 metres at breast height and height 'at least 14 metres', quoted in an Epping Forest District Council 'Favourite Trees' document from a 1998 book (Rogers, Peter: 'Gilwell Park: A Brief History and Guided Tour'), itself citing a nomination from Peter Evans calling it 'a 500 year old fine specimen'. HISTORY: gifted to Scouting founder Robert Baden-Powell in 1919 by Scout Commissioner William de Bois Maclaren as a training centre; Baden-Powell used 'the moral of the acorn and the oak' as an analogy for Scouting's growth from the 1907 Brownsea Island camp; the tree stands at the edge of the Training Ground where the earliest Wood Badge leader-training courses ran from September 1919, and remains a gathering point for the annual Gilwell Reunion. A local legend that Dick Turpin (highwayman, active 1730s, died 1739) hid in the tree is reported by Wikipedia as 'reputed' rather than established; do not state it as fact. Voted England's Tree of the Year 2017 by public vote then UK Tree of the Year by an expert panel, and placed 5th in the European Tree of the Year 2018 with nearly 13,000 votes. LOCATION: treeoftheyear.org's GPS (converted from N51 39'1.14 E0 0'3.83) sits within about 15 metres of the original lead coordinate, so treated as CONFIRMED tree-level; Wikipedia's own coordinate is roughly 80m further east and is likely a rounder, less precise reading of the same park area rather than a different tree. ACCESS is the one open question, see the access field: a stale-looking 2008 council description says appointment-only, the operator's own 2026 visiting page says open drop-in access with reception check-in; delivered as accessible on the newer, more specific, operator-authored source, flagged for anyone who wants to double check before this goes live, since Gilwell Park's core grounds are also a working residential Scout training and camping site.

name: Newton's Apple Tree at MIT
species: Apple, 'Flower of Kent' (Malus domestica 'Flower of Kent')

location.address: The President's Garden, off the Infinite Corridor, MIT campus, 77 Massachusetts Avenue, Cambridge, MA
location.neighbourhood: MIT campus, Cambridge (day-trip distance from central Boston, ~2.9km)

access: Free, no ticket. Stands in the President's Garden off the Infinite Corridor, inside MIT's Main Group of buildings, which a December 2022 Cambridge Day news report (citing an MIT provost/EVP communication) says are open to the general public on weekdays, 6am-7pm, as part of MIT's reopened, historically-open-campus policy; this reopening is dated (Dec 2022) and campus access rules can and do change, so treat the exact hours as indicative rather than guaranteed on the day.
transport: MIT campus, Cambridge, MA; MBTA Red Line to Kendall/MIT station, then a short walk across campus (roughly 10-15 minutes to the Infinite Corridor/President's Garden area).
verify_notes: REVISITING AN EARLIER SAME-DAY VERDICT: this exact candidate is already recorded as 'blocked' in data/leads/_famous-united-states.json (verdict: 'A young graft descended from the Woolsthorpe tree. Significant by lineage, not by age; the same reasoning as the Brown University one.'), apparently from an earlier pass today. My own reading of BRIEF_RESEARCH.md's bar (genuinely old OR visually spectacular OR historically significant, AND publicly accessible) is that a documented living graft-descendant of the actual Newton apple tree, honestly described as a descendant rather than the original, satisfies 'historically significant' on its own, the same way CLAUDE.md's own worked example (the Elm of Saint-Gervais, 'a fallen original honestly succeeded by a living replanting... passes when the entry describes the living tree') allows lineage-based significance without age. DELIVERING THIS AS A FLAGGED CANDIDATE rather than silently overriding the earlier block: the story must describe it plainly as a living descendant grown from cuttings traced through Kew and East Malling, never as 'the' Newton tree. TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES for existence/lineage: MIT's own official facts page (facts.mit.edu, primary institutional source, states the tree 'bears fruit' i.e. alive, present tense, donated by alumnus Ed Vetter Class of 1942, no planting date given) and Tufts University's own 2009 news article, which independently corroborates the MIT tree in detail: Tufts cosmologist Alexander Vilenkin asked MIT physicist Alan Guth about it, MIT president Susan Hockfield personally approved letting Tufts take cuttings, and Tufts' own grounds manager John Vik physically visited MIT and cut three branches from the tree himself in 2009, which is strong independent, dated, on-site corroboration that a real, mature-enough-to-graft-from tree existed at MIT by 2009. AGE: no planting date documented anywhere found; leaving age fields empty per the 'missing age is fine' rule rather than guessing. GIRTH: not found; not recorded. SPECIES: MIT's own page does not name the cultivar. The near-universal identity of Newton-tree descendants worldwide (Cambridge University Botanic Garden's tree, Woolsthorpe's original, and others cited in this pass's searches) is 'Flower of Kent' (Malus domestica), a distinctive old cooking-apple cultivar; used that as the species on the strength of that pattern but this specific identification for the MIT specimen is NOT independently confirmed by an MIT-specific source, so flag it as inferred rather than directly sourced. LOCATION: 'off the Infinite Corridor' in the President's Garden is a real, named campus location, but I found no tree-level coordinate or photograph confirming the precise spot within that garden, so location_precision is approximate, not confirmed; the delivered coordinate is the original lead's own estimate. ACCESS: MIT is famous for an open campus; the Main Group of buildings including the Infinite Corridor were confirmed reopened to the public 6am-7pm weekdays as of a dated Dec 2022 news report, which I fetched directly rather than trusting a search summary; could not independently verify whether the President's Garden itself (an outdoor courtyard) keeps the same hours as the indoor corridor it opens off, or whether policy has shifted again since 2022.
